title: Interpretive canons and their competing rationales
shortTitle: Interpretive canons and their competing rationales
summary: Canons are recurring interpretive principles that draw inferences from language, legal context, or protected institutional values.
notes:
Linguistic canons include ordinary meaning, grammar, giving words significance, associated words, and general language following specific examples. Substantive canons include lenity, constitutional avoidance, clear statements for immunity, and presumptions affecting federal-state relationships. Their justifications differ: some approximate communication practices, while others protect legal values even where drafting practice is uncertain.

Katzmann argues that selection and weighting remain matters of judgment because canons may point in different directions. He credits reliable conventions while questioning a universal ranked code. An index inclusion should identify the particular canon actually used, disputed, or limited in a case rather than associate every statutory case with every canon.
